newsitem.title: USA: Top U.S. antitrust official to mull bankcard suit.
newsitem.headline: Top U.S. antitrust official to mull bankcard suit.

text.p: U.S. Justice Department staff attorneys want to file an antitrust suit against Visa and MasterCard but the final decision will be made by the agency's top antitrust official, sources familiar with the case said Friday.
Staff attorneys want to challenge the bankcard companies' prohibition against their U.S. member banks issuing American Express cards.
The government has spent months examining the practices of Visa and MasterCard.
Acting Justice Department Antitrust Division chief Joel Klein will listen to the arguments of both his staff and the bankcard companies at a meeting set for Feb. 27, the sources said.

American Express, which merchandises its credit card directly to the American public, argues banks should be permitted to issue American Express cards along with Visa and Mastercard, as they are in Europe.

MasterCard and Visa say there is vigorous competition among banks that issue one or both of their cards. They say that to let American Express in would divide the allegiance of the banks in networks they have built up over many years.
Even if the Justice Department were to decide to sue the bankcard companies, the case might not go to trial.
In those instances where the Justice Department has in the past decided to sue, the parties have reached a settlement rather than go to court.
Sources familiar with the case said any talk of settlement was premature as it remained to be seen if Klein would be persuaded to accept the recommendation of his staff.
The staff appeared to have taken to heart the arguments of American Express, the sources said.

"You have the two bankcard associations -- who nominally are competing with each other -- acting in a cartel-like manner to try and monopolize the business," charged Michael O'Neill, senior vice president of public affairs for American Express in New York.
Under current bankcard rules, any bank that wants to carry American Express would have to give up its lucrative MasterCard and Visa business.

But a MasterCard spokeswoman defended the existing system. "We're confident that our position is in the best interest of MasterCard, our cardholders and our members and as such would defend this position vigorously," she said.
